title: Smyrna (Revelation 2:8–11)
hookLine: poor but rich: be faithful unto death

cards: Four words in parentheses hold the heart of today's letter. The King James prints it like this: "I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich)." A poor church, under pressure, about to face worse.
And in the sentence that names their poverty, almost as an aside, a correction: but you're rich.
The second letter goes to the church in Smyrna, and it differs from yesterday's in a way you could miss on a first read: in what isn't said.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO WAS DEAD, AND IS ALIVE.
teach.b: First, who's speaking: "These things saith the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive." Of all the titles from the Patmos vision, this is the one chosen for Smyrna.
To people who may face death, the writer has been through death and come out the other side.

Second, poor but rich. Their poverty is real; the letter doesn't pretend otherwise. But it measures wealth in another currency, as Jesus does in the Gospels with treasure in heaven, where moth and rust don't reach.
The parentheses are small, but they turn the sentence. Third, what's missing. Ephesus got praise and then nevertheless.
Smyrna gets no nevertheless, no rebuke at all.
Only comfort and a warning: "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days."
It doesn't promise escape. Some readers hear the ten days as a limit, and the letter's "I know" tells them they won't face it unseen.

teach.h: FAITHFUL UNTO DEATH: A CROWN OF LIFE.
teach.b: Fourth, the command and the gift: "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."
Some readers note this crown is a victor's wreath, the kind given to someone who finishes a race, rather than a king's crown. Faithful unto death can mean to the point of dying.
It can also mean all the way to the end of a life, one ordinary day after another. The letter closes: "He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death." The first death may come.
The letter says the second will not hurt them.

how: Christians who face poverty or persecution read the letter to Smyrna as words addressed to them, and 'be thou faithful unto death' is read and sung in churches as words of encouragement.

the poor church called rich and given no rebuke

games.q: you're in the church at Smyrna. you're poor, and you're told some of you will be thrown into prison. what does the letter tell you?
o: run, and hide until it's over.
fear none of those things: be faithful unto death.
fight back with everything you have.
games.why: "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer ... be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life." no escape promised: ten days, and a crown.

practice: Think of one small promise nobody is checking on, a call you said you'd make, a habit you started, a person you said you'd look in on, and notice whether it feels heavy or light. Then choose to keep it today, just today.
If you pray, ask for help to be faithful in that one thing; if not, just make the choice quietly.

wordCard.voice: Smyrna. The poor church called rich, given no rebuke, only courage: be faithful unto death, and a crown of life.

orig.note: Greek: a crown or wreath. the word behind 'a crown of life' in Revelation 2:10.

carryVoice: Your line: a crown of life. A wreath for the one who keeps going to the end. See you at the next letter.
